opus-5.5.text:
I think being young is honestly a double-edged sword, and I try to be very clear-eyed about both sides.

On the upside, there's a kind of fearlessness that comes from not yet knowing all the reasons something might fail. When I started working on AI for mathematical reasoning, a lot of people with more experience would say, "Formal verification is too slow," or "Theorem proving is a niche academic problem." And part of me just didn't have the scar tissue to fully believe them. I had spent years doing math competitions and research, and I'd seen firsthand how beautiful and how hard rigorous reasoning is. So it felt natural to say: why not try to build a system that can actually reason the way a mathematician does, and prove it's correct? Being young lets you take a swing at something that sounds unreasonable.

There's also a practical side. Younger founders often have lower opportunity costs. We don't have a long career we're walking away from, and we can afford to move fast, live cheaply, and work very intense hours. In deep tech, where the timeline to real results can be long, that tolerance for uncertainty really matters.

But I don't want to romanticize it. Deep tech is not just about having a bold idea. You need to recruit world-class researchers and engineers, many of whom are older and more accomplished than you. You need to convince investors that you can manage capital responsibly over a multi-year horizon. And you need judgment about which technical bets to make and which to cut, which usually comes from experience. So what I've tried to do is compensate for that gap by surrounding myself with people who are much smarter than me in specific areas, and being very humble about asking for advice.

I'd also say the field itself rewards a certain kind of youth right now. AI is moving so fast that experience from five or ten years ago doesn't always transfer cleanly. In some ways everyone is a beginner again, and that levels the playing field a bit. What matters more is learning speed, intellectual honesty, and the willingness to update quickly when you're wrong.

So my answer is: youth gives you courage and speed, but you have to earn credibility through the quality of your team, your technical depth, and your results. And you have to stay paranoid about your own blind spots.

fable-5.1.text:
I think youth cuts both ways, and I try to be honest about both sides.

The obvious disadvantage is that I haven't spent twenty years inside a research lab or a company watching how things actually get built and sold. There's a kind of pattern recognition you only get from having seen a few cycles, and I don't have that yet. So I compensate by being very deliberate about who I surround myself with. My co-founders and early team include people who have shipped systems at scale and who have deep mathematical training, and I lean on advisors who have been through the hard parts before. I think the worst thing a young founder can do is pretend experience doesn't matter.

But the advantages are real too. First, I'm not anchored to the way things have always been done. When you're working at the intersection of mathematics and AI, the field is moving so fast that a lot of the accumulated wisdom from five years ago is actually a liability. Someone who learned the "right way" to do formal verification in 2015 might have strong instincts that are now wrong. I came in during the moment when large models started to work, so my intuitions were formed in this new regime.

Second, I have an enormous amount of energy and very few obligations. I can work on this problem with total focus for years, and I'm genuinely obsessed with it. Mathematics has been the thing I cared about most since I was a kid competing in olympiads, and the idea that we might build systems that can do real mathematical reasoning feels like the most important problem I could possibly spend my life on. That kind of conviction is hard to manufacture later.

And third, I think the people who are best at frontier research right now are often quite young, because they grew up with these tools. Recruiting them is easier when you speak their language and share their sense of what's possible.

So I'd say readiness isn't really about age. It's about whether you understand the problem deeply, whether you're honest about what you don't know, and whether you can attract people who fill those gaps. I try to hold myself to that standard every day.

astra-6.text:
I think being young cuts both ways. You may have less experience hiring, managing people, or figuring out how a company actually works. And in deep tech, enthusiasm doesn’t substitute for technical depth. You still have to build something that works.

But you also have room to take risks and learn quickly. You might question assumptions that someone with more experience would take for granted. That can be useful, as long as you’re willing to listen when there’s a good reason those assumptions exist.

So I wouldn’t frame readiness primarily around age. I’d ask: Do you understand the problem deeply? Can you bring together people who know things you don’t? And are you willing to change your mind when the evidence tells you to? You don’t need to feel completely ready, but you do need a credible way to close the gaps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think being young cuts both ways. You may have less experience managing people, building a company, or understanding how an industry actually works. And in deep tech, enthusiasm doesn’t replace technical depth, so you have to be honest about what you know and where you need help.

At the same time, you may have more flexibility to take risks and spend years working on a hard problem. You’re also less attached to assumptions about what’s possible. That can be useful, as long as you’re willing to test your ideas and listen when the evidence pushes back.

So I wouldn’t measure readiness by age alone. I’d ask: Do you understand the problem deeply? Can you bring together people who complement you? And are you willing to keep learning when things don’t go as planned?
